title: Fence Colorings
description: A fence has `n` posts and each is painted with one of `k` colours. No three consecutive posts may share the same colour (two adjacent posts may). Return the number of valid colourings.

examples.explanation: Of the 8 colourings of 3 posts, only all-same ones (2 of them) are banned, leaving 6.
A single post can take any of the 5 colours.

title: Frog Energy Path
description: A frog starts on stone 0 and wants to reach the last stone, where `heights[i]` is the height of stone `i`. From stone `i` it may jump to `i + 1` or `i + 2`, spending `|heights[i] - heights[j]|` energy. Return the minimum total energy needed.

examples.explanation: Jump 0 to 1 then 1 to 3 for 20 + 10 = 30 energy.
Jumping 0 to 2, 2 to 4 and 4 to 5 costs 30 + 0 + 10 = 40.

title: Sorted Vowel Strings Count
description: Count the strings of length `n` made only of the vowels `a, e, i, o, u` in which every letter is lexicographically equal to or later than the letter before it. For example `"aeiou"` and `"aae"` qualify but `"ea"` does not.

examples.explanation: Any single vowel works, giving 5 strings.
There are 15 non-decreasing pairs of vowels.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

title: Peak Index In Mountain
description: `arr` strictly increases up to a single peak and then strictly decreases, and the peak is never the first or last element. Return the index of the peak in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: The peak value 5 sits at index 2.
The peak value 3 sits at index 1.

title: Probes To Find Secret
description: A secret number lies in `[1, n]`. You search by repeatedly guessing the middle of the current range `[lo, hi]` using `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` rounded down, then discarding the half that cannot hold it (the guess itself is excluded). Return how many guesses it takes to hit `secret`.

examples.explanation: The guesses are 5, 8, 6 and 7, so 4 probes are needed.
The only guess, 1, is correct.

title: Count Values In Range Sorted
description: `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return how many elements `v` satisfy `lo <= v <= hi`, using binary search.

examples.explanation: The values 3, 3, 5 and 8 lie in [3,8].
No element lies between 7 and 9.

title: Last Occurrence Index
description: `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the largest index `i` with `nums[i] == target`, or `-1` if `target` does not occur. Aim for O(log n).

examples.explanation: The last 2 is at index 3.
The value 4 does not appear.

title: Negatives In Sorted Grid
description: `grid` stores a `rows x cols` matrix in row-major order whose rows and columns are both sorted in non-increasing order. Return how many entries are negative.

examples.explanation: Counting the negatives row by row gives 8.
The grid contains no negative entries.

constraints: Every row and every column is in non-increasing order

title: Closest Value In Sorted Array
description: `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the element of `nums` closest to `target`; if two elements are equally close, return the smaller one.

examples.explanation: 4 and 8 are both 2 away from 6, so the smaller, 4, wins.
5 and 9 are both 2 away from 7, so 5 wins.

title: Gift Pile Remaining
description: `gifts[i]` is the number of gifts in pile `i`. Each second, take the pile with the most gifts (any one if tied) and leave behind `floor(sqrt(pile))` gifts in it, taking the rest. Return how many gifts remain in total after `k` seconds.

examples.explanation: The piles shrink as 100 to 10, 64 to 8, 25 to 5 and 10 to 3, leaving 5, 8, 9, 4, 3.
Each pile of 1 stays at 1.

title: Largest Reduced Pair Product
description: Choose two different indices `i` and `j` of `nums` to maximise `(nums[i] - 1) * (nums[j] - 1)` and return that maximum.

examples.explanation: Using 4 and 5 gives 3 * 4 = 12.
Using both 5s gives 4 * 4 = 16.

title: Fewest Moves To Target
description: You start at `1`. In one move you add `1`, or double the number, but doubling may be used at most `maxDoubles` times in total. Return the minimum number of moves to reach exactly `target`.

examples.explanation: Working back from 19: -1, halve, -1, halve, then three decrements, 7 moves in total.
Working back: 10 to 5 to 4 to 2 to 1 takes 4 moves.

title: Flips To Alternate Bits
description: `s` is a binary string. In one operation you flip any single character. Return the minimum number of operations so that no two adjacent characters are equal.

examples.explanation: Flipping the last character gives "0101".
"10" already alternates.

title: Palindromic Removal Steps
description: `s` contains only the letters `a` and `b`. In one step you delete all characters of some palindromic subsequence of `s` (not necessarily contiguous). Return the minimum number of steps to make `s` empty.

examples.explanation: The whole string is a palindrome, so one step suffices.
Remove the two b's, then the a, for 2 steps.

title: Smallest Four-Digit Split Sum
description: `num` is a four-digit positive integer. Split its digits into two new numbers of two digits each (leading zeros allowed), using every digit exactly once, and return the smallest possible sum of the two numbers.

examples.explanation: Forming 23 and 29 gives the smallest sum, 52.
Forming 04 and 09 gives 13.

title: Raise Digit To Nine
description: `num` is a positive integer made only of the digits `6` and `9`. You may change at most one digit, turning a `6` into a `9` or a `9` into a `6`. Return the largest number you can obtain.

examples.explanation: Changing the first 6 yields 9969.
Changing the final 6 yields 9999.

constraints: num contains only the digits 6 and 9

title: Two Chocolates Leftover
description: You have `money` to spend and must buy exactly two chocolates priced in `prices`. Buy the two cheapest and return the money left over, but if even that pair costs more than `money`, buy nothing and return `money` unchanged.

examples.explanation: The two cheapest cost 1 + 2 = 3, leaving 0.
The cheapest pair costs 5 > 3, so the money is unchanged.

title: Time To Visit All Points
description: `coords` lists points flattened as `x0, y0, x1, y1, ...`. In one second you may move one unit horizontally, vertically, or one unit diagonally (both coordinates change by 1). Return the minimum seconds to visit all points in the given order.

examples.explanation: Moving from (1,1) to (3,4) takes 3 seconds and then to (-1,0) takes 4.
The points differ by 5 horizontally and 0 vertically.

title: Furthest Houses Different Colors
description: `colors[i]` is the colour of house `i`. Return the largest distance `j - i` over pairs `i < j` whose houses have different colours. At least two different colours are present.

examples.explanation: Houses 0 and 3 differ in colour and are 3 apart.
Houses 0 and 4 differ in colour and are 4 apart.

title: Circular Keyboard Typing Time
description: A pointer sits on letter `a` of a circular alphabet `a..z`, where `z` is adjacent to `a`. Moving the pointer one letter in either direction costs 1 second and typing the letter under it costs 1 second. Return the minimum time to type `word`.

examples.explanation: a to b costs 2, b to z costs 3 and z to a costs 2.
Wrapping around the alphabet keeps the moves short and the total is 34.

title: Fewest Clock Adjustments
description: A clock shows `current` minutes after midnight and must be advanced to `target` minutes after midnight (`current <= target`). One operation adds exactly 1, 5, 15 or 60 minutes. Return the minimum number of operations.

examples.explanation: 80 minutes is 60 + 15 + 5, which is 3 operations.
1439 minutes needs 23 hours plus 3 fifteens, 2 fives and 4 ones.

title: Sum Of Closest K Values
description: Pick the `k` elements of `nums` that are closest to `x` by absolute difference, preferring the smaller value when two are equally close, and return their sum. `nums` is not sorted.

examples.explanation: 5 and 7 are each 1 away from 6, and 5 + 7 = 12.
The three 2s are closest and add up to 6.

title: Parity Swap Largest Number
description: You may swap any two digits of `num` that have the same parity (both odd or both even), any number of times. Return the largest integer you can form.

examples.explanation: Odd digits 3,1 and even digits 4,2 are each placed in descending order within their positions.
Odd positions get 7,5,5 and even positions get 8,6.

title: Bags Filled To Capacity
description: Bag `i` holds `rocks[i]` rocks and can hold at most `capacity[i]`. You have `extra` additional rocks to distribute among the bags in any way. Return the maximum number of bags that can be completely full.

examples.explanation: The bags need 1, 1, 0, 1 rocks, so 2 extra rocks fill three bags.
100 extra rocks cover the needs of 8, 0 and 2.

title: Kth Missing Positive Number
description: `arr` is a strictly increasing array of positive integers. Return the `k`-th positive integer (counting from 1) that does not appear in `arr`.

examples.explanation: The missing numbers are 1, 5, 6, 8, 9 and the fifth is 9.
The missing numbers begin 5, 6 and the second is 6.

title: Larger Sign Group Count
description: `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the larger of two counts: how many elements are negative and how many are positive (zeros count for neither).

examples.explanation: There are 3 negatives and 3 positives.
There are 3 negatives and 2 positives.

title: Fewest Elements For Majority
description: Pick the fewest elements of `nums` (as a subset of positions) whose sum is strictly greater than the sum of all the elements left unpicked. Return how many elements you pick.

examples.explanation: 10 + 9 = 19 exceeds the remaining 15.
Two elements reach only 14 of 28, so three (20) are needed.

title: Players And Trainers Matched
description: `players[i]` is the ability of player `i` and `trainers[j]` is the capacity of trainer `j`. A player can be matched to a trainer if `players[i] <= trainers[j]`, and each player and each trainer is used at most once. Return the maximum number of matches.

examples.explanation: Players 4 and 7 match trainers 5 and 8.
Only one trainer exists, so one match at most.

title: Coins From Triple Piles
description: There are `3n` piles of coins. Repeat `n` times: pick any three remaining piles; Alice takes the largest, you take the second largest and Bob takes the smallest. Return the maximum total coins you can collect.

examples.explanation: Triples (1,7,8) and (2,2,4) give you 7 + 2 = 9.
With one triple you take the middle pile, 4.

title: Strings Avoiding 101
description: Count the binary strings of length `n` that do not contain `101` as a contiguous substring.

examples.explanation: Both single-bit strings qualify.
Of the 8 strings of length 3 only "101" is excluded.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

title: Unlimited Trades Profit
description: `prices[i]` is a stock price on day `i`. You may buy and sell as many times as you like, holding at most one share at a time and selling before buying again. Return the maximum total profit.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 and sell at 5, then buy at 3 and sell at 6, for 4 + 3.
Prices only fall, so no trade is made.

title: Fewest Groups Within Spread
description: Split the elements of `nums` into groups (order inside a group does not matter, every element belongs to exactly one group) so that in each group the difference between its largest and smallest value is at most `k`. Return the minimum number of groups.

examples.explanation: Groups {1,2,3} and {5,6} each have spread at most 2.
{1,2} and {3} are needed because 1 and 3 differ by 2.

title: Longest Run Of Open Floors
description: A company rents floors `bottom` to `top` inclusive, and the floors listed in `special` are reserved as relaxation floors. Return the largest number of consecutive floors that are not special.

examples.explanation: Floors 7, 8 and 9 are free in a row.
Every floor in 6..8 is reserved.

constraints: All values of special are distinct

title: Cheapest Falling Path
description: `grid` stores a `rows x cols` matrix in row-major order. A falling path starts at any cell of the first row and moves to the next row each step, landing in the same column or one column to the left or right. Return the minimum possible sum of the cells on such a path from the first to the last row.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Best Non-Negative Product Path
description: `grid` stores a `rows x cols` matrix in row-major order. Travelling from the top-left to the bottom-right and moving only right or down, find the path whose cell product is largest. Return that product modulo `10^9 + 7`, or `-1` if every path has a negative product.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Out of Boundary Paths
description: A ball starts in cell `(startRow, startCol)` of an `m x n` grid and may be moved up, down, left or right, at most `maxMove` times. Count the move sequences of at most `maxMove` moves that push the ball outside the grid (a sequence ends the moment the ball leaves), modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Grid Paths Divisible By K
description: `grid` stores a `rows x cols` matrix in row-major order. Count the paths from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down, whose cell sum is divisible by `k`. Return the count modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Dice Rolls Reaching Target
description: You roll `n` distinguishable dice, each with faces numbered `1` to `k`. Return the number of outcomes whose faces add up to exactly `target`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Delete And Earn Points
description: In one operation you pick a value `v` present in `nums`, earn `v` points for every copy of `v`, and then every copy of `v - 1` and `v + 1` is deleted. Starting with all elements available, return the most points obtainable.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Cheapest Travel Passes
description: You travel on the strictly increasing days listed in `days`. `costs = [c1, c7, c30]` are the prices of passes valid for 1, 7 and 30 consecutive days starting on the day of purchase. Return the minimum total cost to cover every travel day.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

constraints: 1 <= days[i] <= 365 and days is strictly increasing

title: Binary Search Tree Shapes
description: Return the number of structurally different binary search trees that store exactly the keys `1..n`. Two trees are different if their shapes differ.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

title: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence
description: Return the length of the longest subsequence of `nums` (elements kept in their original order, not necessarily adjacent) in which consecutive elements differ by one constant amount.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Largest Subset Within Budget Of Zeros And Ones
description: `words` is a string of binary words separated by single spaces. Choose a subset of the words that uses at most `m` zero characters and at most `n` one characters in total. Return the largest number of words you can choose.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

constraints: 1 <= number of words <= 600, each word has 1 to 10 characters from `0` and `1`

title: Smash Stones Remainder
description: `stones[i]` is the weight of a stone. Repeatedly pick any two stones `x <= y` and smash them: if `x == y` both vanish, otherwise a single stone of weight `y - x` remains. You may choose the pairs in any order. Return the smallest possible weight of the last remaining stone, or `0` if none remains.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Split Into K Equal Sum Groups
description: Return `true` if the elements of `nums` can be divided into exactly `k` non-empty groups, every element used exactly once, so that all groups have the same sum.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Pick Numbers To Reach Total
description: Two players alternately pick an unused integer from `1..maxChoosable` (no number is picked twice) and add it to a running total; whoever first makes the total reach at least `desiredTotal` wins. Both play optimally and the first player moves first. Return `true` if the first player wins; if even all numbers together cannot reach `desiredTotal`, nobody wins and the answer is `false`.

examples.explanation: TBD
TBD

title: Smallest Dominating Subsequence Size
description: Choose some elements of `nums` so that their sum is strictly greater than the sum of all the elements left unchosen. Return the smallest number of elements you must choose.

examples.explanation: Picking the largest elements first gives a minimum of 2 chosen element(s) whose sum beats the rest.
Picking the largest elements first gives a minimum of 3 chosen element(s) whose sum beats the rest.

title: Minimum Rounds To Finish Tasks
description: `tasks[i]` is the difficulty level of task `i`. In one round you may finish either 2 or 3 tasks that all share the same difficulty. Return the fewest rounds needed to finish every task, or -1 if that is impossible.

examples.explanation: Each difficulty group is cleared in groups of 2 or 3, giving 4 in total (or -1 when some level has one task).
Each difficulty group is cleared in groups of 2 or 3, giving -1 in total (or -1 when some level has one task).

title: Best Alternating Pick Sum
description: Pick a non-empty subsequence of `nums` and score it by adding its 1st, 3rd, 5th, ... chosen elements and subtracting its 2nd, 4th, ... chosen elements. Return the maximum score over all non-empty subsequences.

examples.explanation: The best sign-alternating pick scores 7.
The best sign-alternating pick scores 8.

title: Days To Eat All Oranges
description: There are `n` oranges. Each day you do exactly one of: eat one orange; if `n` is divisible by 2, eat `n / 2` of them; if `n` is divisible by 3, eat `2 * (n / 3)` of them. Return the minimum number of days to eat all `n` oranges.

examples.explanation: The cheapest sequence of daily choices needs 4 day(s).
The cheapest sequence of daily choices needs 3 day(s).

constraints: Each day exactly one of the three actions is used

title: Minimum Starting Health
description: `grid` stores a `rows x cols` matrix in row-major order; entering a cell adds its value to your health. You start in the top-left cell and move only right or down to the bottom-right cell. Return the minimum starting health so that your health is at least 1 after entering every cell on your path, including the first and last.

examples.explanation: The safest route needs an initial health of 7.
The safest route needs an initial health of 1.

title: Route With Free Passes
description: `grid` stores a `rows x cols` matrix in row-major order, where each cell has a toll. Travel from the top-left to the bottom-right cell moving only right or down, paying the toll of every cell you enter plus the first cell. You hold `k` free passes, each of which waives the toll of one cell on your route. Return the minimum total toll.

examples.explanation: Spending the free passes on the costliest cells of the best route leaves a toll of 7.
Spending the free passes on the costliest cells of the best route leaves a toll of 3.

title: Cheapest Polygon Triangulation
description: `values[i]` is the label of the `i`-th vertex of a convex polygon listed in order. Split the polygon into triangles using non-crossing diagonals; each triangle costs the product of its three vertex labels. Return the minimum total cost of a triangulation.

examples.explanation: The best set of diagonals costs 6 in total.
The best set of diagonals costs 144 in total.

title: Smallest Leaf-Product Tree
description: `leaves` lists, in order, the values of the leaves of a binary tree in which every internal node has exactly two children. The value of an internal node is the product of the largest leaf in its left subtree and the largest leaf in its right subtree. Over all such trees that keep the leaves in this order, return the minimum possible sum of the internal node values.

examples.explanation: Merging the smallest neighbouring leaves first gives a total of 32.
Merging the smallest neighbouring leaves first gives a total of 44.

title: Cheapest Stick Cutting
description: A wooden stick has length `n`, with marks at positions `1..n-1`. `cuts` lists distinct positions where you must cut, in any order you choose. Each cut costs the current length of the piece being cut. Return the minimum total cost.

examples.explanation: Choosing the cutting order well gives a minimum total cost of 16.
Choosing the cutting order well gives a minimum total cost of 22.

title: Fair Cookie Distribution
description: `cookies[i]` is the number of cookies in bag `i`. Every bag must be handed whole to exactly one of `k` children. The unfairness of a distribution is the largest total any single child receives. Return the minimum possible unfairness.

examples.explanation: The most balanced split leaves the busiest child with 31 cookies.
The most balanced split leaves the busiest child with 7 cookies.

title: Divisible Position Arrangements
description: Count the permutations `p` of the numbers `1..n` such that for every 1-indexed position `i`, either `p[i]` is divisible by `i` or `i` is divisible by `p[i]`.

examples.explanation: Exactly 2 permutation(s) satisfy the divisibility rule at every position.
Exactly 3 permutation(s) satisfy the divisibility rule at every position.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit integer

title: Numbers From Allowed Digits
description: `digits` is a sorted list of distinct digits from 1 to 9. Count the positive integers less than or equal to `n` whose decimal representation uses only digits from `digits` (each digit may repeat).

examples.explanation: Counting numbers by length and prefix gives 20 valid number(s).
Counting numbers by length and prefix gives 29523 valid number(s).

constraints: digits is sorted, distinct, each in 1..9

title: Longest Shared Block
description: Given two integer arrays `a` and `b`, return the length of the longest contiguous block of elements that appears in both arrays (in the same order). Return 0 if they share no element.

examples.explanation: The longest run common to both arrays has length 3.
The longest run common to both arrays has length 5.

title: Cheapest Deletions To Match Strings
description: You may delete characters from either of the strings `s` and `t`, and deleting a character costs its ASCII value. Return the minimum total cost needed to make the two strings identical (both may become empty).

examples.explanation: Keeping the heaviest common subsequence leaves a deletion cost of 231.
Keeping the heaviest common subsequence leaves a deletion cost of 403.

constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters

title: Cheapest House Painting
description: A street has `n` houses in a row, each to be painted one of 3 colours, where `costs[3*i + c]` is the cost of painting house `i` with colour `c`. Two neighbouring houses must not share a colour. Return the minimum total cost to paint all houses.

examples.explanation: The cheapest valid colouring costs 10.
The cheapest valid colouring costs 2.

title: Tilings Of A Two-Row Strip
description: A 2 x `n` board is tiled completely with 2x1 dominoes (either orientation) and L-shaped trominoes (any rotation); pieces cannot overlap or hang off the board. Return the number of distinct tilings modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: There are 5 distinct tilings (modulo 1000000007).
There are 1 distinct tilings (modulo 1000000007).

constraints: Two tilings differ if some pair of cells is covered by a piece in one but not in the other

title: Phone Pad Knight Walks
description: A chess knight stands on a phone keypad (rows `1 2 3`, `4 5 6`, `7 8 9`, and a bottom row with only `0` under `8`). It starts on any digit and makes `n - 1` knight moves, always landing on a key, dialing each digit it visits. Return how many distinct digit sequences of length `n` it can dial, modulo 1000000007.

examples.explanation: The knight can dial 10 different numbers of length n (modulo 1000000007).
The knight can dial 20 different numbers of length n (modulo 1000000007).

constraints: A knight move changes position by (+-1, +-2) or (+-2, +-1) keys

title: Three-Stone Pick Game Winner
description: `values[i]` is the value of the `i`-th stone in a row. Alice and Bob alternate, Alice first; on a turn a player takes 1, 2 or 3 stones from the front of the row. Both play to maximise their own total. Return `"Alice"` or `"Bob"` for the player with the larger total, or `"Tie"` if equal.

examples.explanation: With optimal play the result is Bob.
With optimal play the result is Alice.

title: Max Points With Column Penalty
description: `grid` stores a `rows x cols` matrix in row-major order. Choose exactly one cell in every row and add up their values, then subtract `|c1 - c2|` for every pair of chosen cells in adjacent rows lying in columns `c1` and `c2`. Return the maximum score.

examples.explanation: The best choice of one cell per row scores 9.
The best choice of one cell per row scores 8.

title: Rebuild Queue From Heights
description: People stand in a queue; `people` is a flat array of pairs where `people[2*i]` is person `i`'s height and `people[2*i+1]` is how many people standing in front of them are at least that tall. Rebuild the (unique) queue that satisfies every pair and return the heights from front to back as a comma-separated string.

examples.explanation: Placing tallest people first and inserting by count gives heights 5,7,5,6,4,7.
Placing tallest people first and inserting by count gives heights 4,5,2,3,1,6.

constraints: A valid queue is guaranteed to exist

title: Largest Non-Decreasing Digits Number
description: Given a non-negative integer `n`, return the largest integer that is less than or equal to `n` and whose decimal digits are in non-decreasing order from left to right.

examples.explanation: The largest such number not exceeding n is 9.
The largest such number not exceeding n is 1234.

title: Most Courses Before Deadlines
description: `courses` is a flat array of pairs: `courses[2*i]` is the number of days course `i` takes and `courses[2*i+1]` is the last day by which it must be finished. Courses are taken one at a time starting on day 1 with no gaps or overlap. Return the maximum number of courses that can be completed.

examples.explanation: Dropping the longest course whenever time runs out lets 3 course(s) finish.
Dropping the longest course whenever time runs out lets 1 course(s) finish.

title: Nth Prime-Limited Number
description: A number is `primes`-limited if its only prime factors are among the numbers in `primes` (1 counts as primes-limited). Return the `n`-th smallest primes-limited number, counting 1 as the first.

examples.explanation: Merging multiples of the allowed primes in order gives 32 as the n-th such number.
Merging multiples of the allowed primes in order gives 1 as the n-th such number.

constraints: 1 <= primes.length <= 10, primes are distinct, sorted ascending, each prime <= 100
1 <= n <= 10^4, and the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

title: Integers Without Adjacent Set Bits
description: Count the integers `x` with `0 <= x <= n` whose binary representation contains no two adjacent 1 bits.

examples.explanation: Exactly 5 integer(s) in [0, n] have no two adjacent set bits.
Exactly 2 integer(s) in [0, n] have no two adjacent set bits.

constraints: x is counted in its plain binary form without leading zeros

title: Count Valid Rotated Numbers
description: Rotating a digit by 180 degrees maps 0, 1, 8 to themselves, 2 to 5, 5 to 2, 6 to 9, 9 to 6, and any other digit becomes invalid. A positive integer is valid if every digit rotates to a digit and the rotated number differs from the original. Return how many integers in `[1, n]` are valid.

examples.explanation: Exactly 4 number(s) up to n change when rotated.
Exactly 0 number(s) up to n change when rotated.

constraints: Rotated numbers are read digit by digit, so leading zeros never arise

title: Longest Equal Ribbon Pieces
description: `ribbons[i]` is the length of the `i`-th ribbon. Cut the ribbons (no joining) into pieces of one common positive integer length so that you obtain at least `k` pieces; leftovers are discarded. Return the largest possible piece length, or 0 if even length 1 pieces cannot reach `k`.

examples.explanation: The longest common piece length that yields enough pieces is 5.
The longest common piece length that yields enough pieces is 4.

title: Minimize Largest After Shifting Left
description: In one operation pick an index `i >= 1` with `nums[i] > 0`, decrease `nums[i]` by 1 and increase `nums[i-1]` by 1. After any number of operations, return the minimum possible value of the largest element of `nums`.

examples.explanation: Pushing surplus leftwards as evenly as possible leaves a maximum of 5.
Pushing surplus leftwards as evenly as possible leaves a maximum of 10.

title: Tallest Peak Under Sum Cap
description: Build an array of `n` positive integers in which adjacent elements differ by at most 1 and the total sum is at most `maxSum`. Return the largest value that element at position `index` (0-indexed) can have.

examples.explanation: The element at the given index can reach at most 2.
The element at the given index can reach at most 3.

title: Most Removable Characters
description: `p` is a subsequence of `s`. `removable` lists distinct indices of `s`; deleting characters at the first `k` indices of `removable` (all at once) must keep `p` a subsequence of what remains. Return the largest such `k`.

examples.explanation: Removing the first 2 listed position(s) still leaves the pattern as a subsequence.
Removing the first 1 listed position(s) still leaves the pattern as a subsequence.

constraints: 0 <= removable.length <= s.length, removable has distinct valid indices
s and p consist of lowercase English letters

title: Boxes Removal Best Score
description: Boxes in a row are coloured by `boxes`. In one move you remove any block of `k` consecutive boxes that all share one colour and earn `k * k` points; the remaining boxes close up. Return the maximum total points for removing every box.

examples.explanation: Removing blocks in the best order earns 23 points.
Removing blocks in the best order earns 9 points.

title: Paint Houses Neighborhood Cost
description: A row of `m` houses can each be painted one of `n` colours (numbered `1..n`). `houses[i]` is `0` if house `i` is unpainted, otherwise its fixed colour. `cost` is a flat array where painting house `i` colour `c` costs `cost[i * n + (c - 1)]`. A neighbourhood is a maximal run of adjacent houses with the same colour. Return the minimum cost to paint all unpainted houses so that there are exactly `target` neighbourhoods, or `-1` if impossible.

examples.explanation: The cheapest painting with exactly the required neighbourhoods costs 9 (-1 means impossible).
The cheapest painting with exactly the required neighbourhoods costs 11 (-1 means impossible).

constraints: houses.length = m, cost.length = m * n, 0 <= houses[i] <= n

title: Exam Seating Capacity
description: A classroom is an `R x C` grid stored row by row in `seats`; `1` is a usable seat and `0` is broken. No two students may sit in horizontally adjacent seats, and no two may sit in seats that are diagonally adjacent across consecutive rows (a student can see left, right, upper-left and upper-right). Return the maximum number of students that can be seated.

examples.explanation: At most 4 students can be seated without any of them seeing each other.
At most 1 students can be seated without any of them seeing each other.

title: Dungeon Minimum Starting Health
description: A knight starts in the top-left of an `R x C` dungeon stored row by row in `grid` and must reach the bottom-right, moving only right or down. Each cell changes his health by `grid[i]` (negative = damage). His health must stay at least `1` at all times, including after the first and last cells. Return the minimum starting health that makes the trip possible.

examples.explanation: The knight needs at least 7 starting health.
The knight needs at least 1 starting health.

title: Round-Trip Cherry Pickup
description: An `R x C` field is stored row by row in `grid`: `1` is a cherry, `0` is an empty cell and `-1` is a thorn you cannot step on. Walk from the top-left to the bottom-right moving only right or down, then walk back to the top-left moving only left or up, picking up each cherry at most once (picked cells become empty). If no valid round trip exists, return `0`. Otherwise return the maximum number of cherries collected.

examples.explanation: The best round trip collects 5 cherries (0 if the field cannot be crossed).
The best round trip collects 0 cherries (0 if the field cannot be crossed).

title: Cheapest Stick Cutting Order
description: A stick of length `n` must be cut at every position listed in `cuts` (measured from the left end), in any order you choose. Each cut costs the current length of the piece being cut. Return the minimum total cost of all cuts.

examples.explanation: Choosing the cutting order well gives a total cost of 16.
Choosing the cutting order well gives a total cost of 22.

title: Profitable Crime Schemes
description: Crime `i` needs `group[i]` members and pays `profit[i]`. A member can join only one crime. A scheme is any subset of crimes (the empty subset counts) whose combined profit is at least `minProfit` and whose total members is at most `n`. Return the number of schemes modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: 2 subsets of crimes use at most n members and reach the required profit.
7 subsets of crimes use at most n members and reach the required profit.

title: Count Valid Playlists
description: A playlist has exactly `goal` songs (repeats allowed) chosen from `n` different songs. Every song must be played at least once, and a song may be played again only after at least `k` other songs have been played since its previous play. Return the number of valid playlists modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: There are 6 valid playlists.
There are 6 valid playlists.

title: Count Rewardable Attendance Records
description: An attendance record of length `n` uses `A` (absent), `L` (late) and `P` (present). It earns an award if it has fewer than two `A`s in total and never three or more consecutive `L`s. Return the number of award-earning records of length `n`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: Exactly 3 records of this length earn the award.
Exactly 8 records of this length earn the award.

title: Fewest Window Bit Flips
description: `nums` contains only 0s and 1s. In one move you pick `k` consecutive elements and flip every bit in them (0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0). Return the minimum number of moves so that no 0 remains, or `-1` if that is impossible.

examples.explanation: The minimum number of window flips is 2 (-1 means impossible).
The minimum number of window flips is -1 (-1 means impossible).

title: Best Value With K Events
description: `events` is a flat array of triples: `events[3*i]` is the first day, `events[3*i+1]` the last day (inclusive) and `events[3*i+2]` the value of event `i`. You may attend at most `k` events, and you cannot attend two events whose day ranges overlap (an event ending on day `d` blocks one starting on day `d`). Return the maximum total value.

examples.explanation: The best choice of at most k non-overlapping events is worth 7.
The best choice of at most k non-overlapping events is worth 10.

title: Fairest Job Distribution
description: `jobs[i]` is the time job `i` takes. Assign every job to exactly one of `k` workers. A worker's workload is the total time of their jobs. Return the smallest possible value of the largest workload.

examples.explanation: The most balanced assignment has a largest workload of 3.
The most balanced assignment has a largest workload of 11.

title: Fewest Numbers To Patch In
description: `nums` is sorted in ascending order. Add (patch) as few new positive integers as needed so that every integer from `1` to `n` can be written as the sum of some elements of the resulting array (each element used at most once). Return the minimum number of patches.

examples.explanation: 1 extra number(s) must be added to reach every sum up to n.
2 extra number(s) must be added to reach every sum up to n.

title: Best Score From Both Ends
description: You perform `multipliers.length` operations in order. In operation `i` you take either the first or the last remaining element `x` of `nums` (removing it) and gain `multipliers[i] * x`. Return the maximum total score.

examples.explanation: The best sequence of end-picks scores 14.
The best sequence of end-picks scores 102.

title: Tallest Twin Support Pillars
description: You have steel rods with lengths in `rods`. Two support pillars must have exactly the same height; each pillar is built by welding together a disjoint subset of the rods (a rod may also be left unused). Return the largest possible height of the pillars, or `0` if no two equal pillars of positive height can be built.

examples.explanation: The tallest pair of equal pillars has height 6.
The tallest pair of equal pillars has height 10.

title: Fewest Hops With Same-Value Portals
description: You start at index 0 of `arr`. In one hop you may move to `i + 1`, to `i - 1`, or to any index `j != i` where `arr[j] == arr[i]`. You can never leave the array. Return the minimum number of hops to reach the last index.

examples.explanation: The shortest route to the last index takes 3 hops.
The shortest route to the last index takes 0 hops.

title: Longest Descending Hop Chain
description: From index `i` of `arr` you may hop to an index `j` with `0 < |i - j| <= d` only if `arr[i] > arr[j]` and `arr[i]` is also greater than every value strictly between `i` and `j`. You may start anywhere. Return the maximum number of indices you can visit in one chain of hops (counting the start).

examples.explanation: The longest chain of hops visits 4 indices.
The longest chain of hops visits 1 indices.

title: Count Arithmetic Subsequences
description: Count the subsequences of `nums` with at least three elements in which consecutive elements differ by the same constant. Two subsequences are different if they use different index sets, even when their values are equal. Return the count modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: There are 7 arithmetic subsequences of length 3 or more.
There are 16 arithmetic subsequences of length 3 or more.

title: Three-Stone Pile Duel
description: Alice and Bob alternate turns, Alice first, on a row of stone piles with values `values`. On a turn the player takes 1, 2 or 3 piles from the front of the row and adds their values to their own score (values can be negative). Both play to maximise their own final score. Return Alice's final score minus Bob's final score.

examples.explanation: With optimal play, Alice's score minus Bob's score is -1.
With optimal play, Alice's score minus Bob's score is 15.

title: Best Like-Time Dish Order
description: A chef can cook any subset of dishes in any order, spending one unit of time per dish. If a dish with satisfaction `s` is cooked as the `t`-th dish (`t` starts at 1), it adds `t * s` to the like-time coefficient. Return the maximum like-time coefficient over all choices of dishes and orders (the empty choice gives `0`).

examples.explanation: The best order of dishes gives a like-time coefficient of 14.
The best order of dishes gives a like-time coefficient of 20.

title: Fewest Column Swaps To Increase
description: `a` and `b` have the same length. In one move you may swap `a[i]` with `b[i]` at the same index `i`. Return the minimum number of moves that makes both `a` and `b` strictly increasing. The input is guaranteed to have a solution.

examples.explanation: The minimum number of same-index swaps is 1.
The minimum number of same-index swaps is 1.

constraints: 0 <= a[i], b[i] <= 2 * 10^5, a solution always exists

title: Fewest Replacements To Strictly Increasing
description: In one operation you may replace any element of `arr1` with any element of `arr2` (an element of `arr2` can be reused any number of times). Return the minimum number of operations that makes `arr1` strictly increasing, or `-1` if that is impossible.

examples.explanation: The minimum number of replacements is 1 (-1 means impossible).
The minimum number of replacements is 2 (-1 means impossible).

title: Fewest Rounds To Balance Machines
description: `machines[i]` is the number of dresses in washing machine `i` (machines stand in a line). In one round you pick any subset of machines and each chosen machine passes exactly one of its dresses to one adjacent machine, all at the same moment. Return the minimum number of rounds to give every machine the same number of dresses, or `-1` if that is impossible.

examples.explanation: Balancing the machines needs 3 rounds (-1 means impossible).
Balancing the machines needs 2 rounds (-1 means impossible).

title: Most Points Rotation Index
description: Rotating `nums` by `k` means moving the first `k` elements, in order, to the end. After a rotation, an element scores one point if its value is less than or equal to its new index. Every value of `nums` is smaller than `nums.length`. Return the rotation `k` (0 <= k < n) that gives the highest total points; if several tie, return the smallest `k`.

examples.explanation: Rotation 3 gives the most points (smallest such k).
Rotation 0 gives the most points (smallest such k).

title: Least Time To Clear Illegal Cars
description: A train is described by the string `s`; `'1'` marks a car carrying illegal goods and `'0'` a clean car. In one operation you may remove the leftmost car (cost 1), the rightmost car (cost 1), or any car from the middle (cost 2). Return the minimum total cost to remove every car carrying illegal goods; clean cars may stay.

examples.explanation: The cheapest way to remove every illegal car costs 5.
The cheapest way to remove every illegal car costs 2.
